articles_hidden.title: Engineering signalling centres to trigger human trunk morphogenesis in vitro
articles_hidden.authors: Tianlei He, Steven Zwick, Yusuf Ilker Yaman, Alon Chappleboim, Josephine Johnston, David A. Weitz, Sharad Ramanathan
articles_hidden.abstract: Vertebrate trunk development is orchestrated by endogenous signalling centres that generate gradients of signals such as WNT and BMP to pattern cell fates and drive morphogenesis1,2,3,4,5,6,7. Whether these cues alone can reconstitute human trunk-like morphogenesis in vitro remains unknown. Here we present a synthetic embryology platform for high-throughput, spatiotemporal delivery of morphogen signals to epithelial cysts derived from human pluripotent stem cells. Transient WNT and BMP gradients are sufficient to drive the generation of axially elongating trunk-like structures that contain a central neural tube flanked by axial, paraxial, intermediate and lateral mesoderm. The geometry of the transient BMP signal exerts lasting control over mediolateral patterning and bilateral symmetry. Patterning and morphogenesis are sustained by neuromesodermal and lateral plate mesoderm progenitors induced by the initial cues, which act as endogenous signalling centres. Together, these findings define a minimal spatial code sufficient to reconstitute trunk-like morphogenesis in a human stem-cell-based model and establish a scalable platform for studying early human development and congenital disorders.

articles_hidden.title: An enduring climatic burden from past peatland drainage
articles_hidden.authors: Jevan B. Yu, Etienne Fluet-Chouinard, Susan E. Page, Chris D. Evans, Charles F. Harvey, César Terrer
articles_hidden.abstract: Over millennia, peatlands have removed hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere but emitted a proportion back as methane (CH4), exerting a slow net cooling effect1. Artificial drainage of these ecosystemsâ€”a centuries-old practice2,3â€”causes decomposition and the re-release of CO2 but suppresses CH4 emissions4, with a net climatic effect that is not well quantified at the global scale5. Here we reconstructed the radiative forcing from worldwide peatland drainage over 1800â€“2020 by combining a new flux dataset, hydrologically driven models of CO2 and CH4 fluxes and a hindcast of drainage extent and intensity. We found that drainage has produced a net heating effect of +73â€‰(48â€“99)â€‰mWâ€‰mâˆ’2â€”equivalent to 2.7â€‰(1.8â€“3.6)% of industrial-era radiative forcingâ€”originating from 0.4â€“0.5% of global land area. The net heating results from the dominant forcing of drainage-induced CO2 emissions (+83â€‰(52â€“110)â€‰mWâ€‰mâˆ’2) over that of avoided CH4 emissions (âˆ’9â€‰(âˆ’15â€“âˆ’2)â€‰mWâ€‰mâˆ’2). Even without further expansion of drainage, maintaining currently drained areas could almost double the cumulative warming by 2100. Our reconstruction captures the opposing impacts of peatland drainage on global budgets of CO2 and CH4 and quantifies the strong legacy effects of historical drainage on present and possibly future climate.

articles_hidden.title: Clinical landscape of cardiometabolic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
articles_hidden.authors: Gabriele G. Schiattarella, Joseph A. Hill
articles_hidden.abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) has emerged as the predominant form of heart failure worldwide and is increasingly associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes and systemic cardiometabolic dysfunction. This cardiometabolic HFpEF entity can be conceptualized as a mechanistically defined endotype marked by endothelial dysfunction, metabolic inflexibility and maladaptive inter-organ signalling involving the liver, kidney, adipose tissue and skeletal muscle. The cardiometabolic endotype often corresponds to a clinically recognizable adiposity-related clinical phenotype. Despite the growing prevalence of cardiometabolic HFpEF, therapeutic progress has lagged. This is mostly because the classification structure used is based on a commonly over-interpreted biomarkerâ€”ejection fractionâ€”although inadequate trial end points and a lack of mechanism-guided precision also have a role. Here we review the evolving epidemiology, mechanistic underpinnings and emerging therapeutic landscape of cardiometabolic HFpEF. We highlight limitations in current diagnostic criteria, the role of extracardiac drivers and the need for soft end points and systems-based modelling. Advances in '-omics', phenotyping and cross-disciplinary frameworks now offer a pathway towards mechanistically targeted interventions that could enable symptomatic control by modifying validated disease mechanisms that culminate in this syndrome.

articles_hidden.title: Middle–Late Pleistocene Denisovans and unresolved Homo in southern China
articles_hidden.authors: Song Xing, Huiyun Rao, Guangmao Xie, Fan Bai, Junyi Ge, E. Andrew Bennett, Zhongyou Wu, Qingfeng Shao, Xianglei Li, Bence Viola, Qiyahui Sun, Kai Zhou, Zitao Li, Qigao Jiangzuo, Yuhao Zhao, Feng Liu, Yingjie Liu, Xiaotian Feng, Qiang Lin, Qiaomei Fu
articles_hidden.abstract: Molecular and morphological evidence increasingly supports the view that most East Asian Middle to Late Pleistocene archaic Homo belong to Denisovans1, yet the presence of other contemporaneous lineages has remained unclear. Here we report a set of newly discovered hominin fossils (4 isolated teeth; more than 100.8 thousand years ago and 104.5â€“42.6 thousand years ago, respectively) from 2 cave sites (Chuanshandong and Longchuandong) in Guangxi, southern China. Integrated morphological and palaeoproteomic analyses reveal substantial phenotypic and molecular diversity consistent with at least two distinct lineages. One lineage (Longchuandong) is assigned to a Denisovan-affinity population, owing to its extreme similarity to Altai Denisovans with respect to dental morphology and single amino acid polymorphisms that match those of Denisovans from Harbin, Penghu, Bianfu Cave and Altai. The other lineage, represented by the Chuanshandong hominin, is an unresolved archaic Homo, as it carries an ancestral variant (AMELY 179M) shared with Homo antecessor and great apes and another variant (AMBN 253G) that is diagnostic of East Asian Middle Pleistocene Homo erectus but lacks the Denisovan-associated AMBN 273V variant (it being highly probable that this is inherited from H. erectus). Dental morphology in this lineage exhibits a mosaic of plesiomorphic and derived traits but no clear Denisovan affinity. These findings indicate that diverse hominin populations may have inhabited subtropical China during theÂ Middle and Late Pleistocene, including a Denisovan-affinity population and another unresolved archaic Homo.

articles_hidden.title: Coherent parity oscillations in coupled minimal Kitaev chains
articles_hidden.authors: Francesco Zatelli, Bart Roovers, Nick van Loo, Antonio Lombardi, Juan D. Torres Luna, Sebastian Miles, Vincent P. M. Sietses, Florian J. Bennebroek Evertsz’, Pablo Cova Fariña, Alberto Bordin, Ghada Badawy, Erik P. A. M. Bakkers, Michael Wimmer, Leo P. Kouwenhoven
articles_hidden.abstract: Majorana zero modes provide a route to fault-tolerant qubits by encoding information non-locally in fermion parity. Their noise sensitivity is expected to decrease exponentially with separation between Majorana zero modes, a suppression known as topological protection1. Kitaev chains in quantum-dotâ€“superconductor arrays can host Majorana zero modes at their ends1,2, even in two-site chains3. These minimal-chain modes, known as poor manâ€™s Majoranas, retain characteristic Majorana properties, including near-zero energy and equal electronâ€“hole character, but lack topological protection3,4,5. A key challenge is moving from identifying these modes in electrical transport to coherent qubit control. Here we demonstrate coherent time-resolved rotations between parity states encoded by four poor manâ€™s Majoranas in two coupled minimal Kitaev chains3,6,7,8. Total fermion parity conservation separates the system into global even- and odd-parity manifolds. We observe coherent parity oscillations in both, with frequencies matching within 5% at the poor manâ€™s Majorana sweet spot, consistent with largely isolated Majoranas6. The oscillation frequency, rotation axis and coherence depend systematically on inter-chain coupling and quantum-dot detunings, in agreement with our model for short chains. Our results establish coherent control of a qubit encoded in the fermion parity of Majorana zero modes, realized using minimal Kitaev chains. They lay the groundwork for universal qubit operations, comprehensive coherence characterization and probing protection in longer chains.

articles_hidden.title: Single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map for coronary artery disease
articles_hidden.authors: Junedh M. Amrute, Paul C. Lee, Ittai Eres, Tracy Yamawaki, Chang Jie Mick Lee, Maharshi Chakraborty, Andrea Bredemeyer, Maya U. Sheth, Quanyi Zhao, Trieu Nguyen, Eric Yuan, Hannah C. Plunkett Paletta, Yizhou Wang, Rijan Gurung, Chukwuemeka Anene-Nzelu, Wen-Ling Lin, Wei-Lin Qiu, Xue Liang, Yuntian Zhang, Cassia Williams-Rogers, Joohee Oh, Jixin Cui, Roland S. Wu, Ruth Gómez Graciani, Wei Qiang Seow, Soumya Kundu, Daniel Y. Li, Markus Ramste, Daniel R. Lu, Anthony Tan, Chul Joo Kang, Ryan E. Wagoner, Arturo Alisio, Sikander Hayat, Daniel Kreisel, Kory J. Miller, Boxiang Liu, Scott Martin, Simon Jackson, Robin Andersson, Jesse M. Engreitz, Roger S-Y Foo, Chi-Ming Li, Brandon Ason, Thomas Quertermous, Nathan O. Stitziel
articles_hidden.abstract: Although coronary artery disease (CAD) genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci, most variants lie in non-coding regions, obscuring the causal gene programmes and cell types driving disease1,2. Here we performed single-nucleus multi-omic profiling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility in human coronary arteries from 44 people to construct a genome-wide single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map. We identified 11,269 chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTLs) across principal vascular cell types, including CAD-associated caQTLs in smooth muscle cells (SMCs). Using dynamic single-cell caQTL modelling3, we show that variant effects on chromatin vary across SMC states. For example, rs658956-mediated suppression ofÂ the FGGY-DT enhancer through disruption of an AP-1 motif is amplified as SMCs transition towards a fibromyocyte fate. We next performed genome-wide high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) in 15 human coronary arteries, showing that rs4887091 in the ADAMTS7 CAD locus has allele-dependent effects on CCCTC-binding factor occupancy and loop strength. Integrating Hi-C, Hi-C with chromatin immunoprecipitation and in vitro clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats interferenceÂ (CRISPRi) nominated AMOTL2 as a distal SMC-specific CAD gene whose loss promotes proliferation and suppresses contractile identity. Finally, arrayed Perturbâ€“seq of GWAS-nominated enhancers converged on extracellular matrix remodelling as a core SMC disease programme. Together, these findings provide a framework for mapping non-coding GWAS variants to cell types, chromatin states and gene programmes in human disease.

articles_hidden.title: A gut–brain sensory-motor circuit regulates sugar ingestion in Drosophila
articles_hidden.authors: Xinyue Cui, Matthew R. Meiselman, Staci N. Thornton, Sophia Gustin, Jennifer Jeter, Geoffrey W. Meissner, Nilay Yapici
articles_hidden.abstract: Bidirectional communication between the brain and digestive tract is critical for optimizing nutrient preference and food intake, yet the neural mechanisms that couple gut nutrient sensing with ingestive motor control remain poorly understood. Here we identify a gutâ€“brain sensory-motor circuit that regulates sugar ingestion in flies. We show that the brain neurons that regulate food ingestion, IN1s1, receive excitatory input from enteric sensory neurons that penetrate the foregut epithelium and detect sugars in the gut lumen during ingestion. Functional imaging and connectome analyses reveal that IN1s integrate excitatory input from multiple sugar-sensing neurons, including enteric sensory neurons, and provide inhibitory output to enteric motor neurons that control the muscles at the entry of the cropâ€”a stomach-like organ. During ingestion, IN1 activation suppresses these enteric motor neurons, relaxes the crop duct and promotes rapid transfer of food into the crop, thereby enabling sustained food intake. Together, our findings describe a gutâ€“brain circuit that controls the motor activity of digestive tract muscles during feeding and suggest a circuit mechanism by which nutrient signals from the gut contribute to the dynamic regulation of food intake across metabolic states.

articles_hidden.title: Heterogeneity co-evolves with architecture to determine colon cancer outcome
articles_hidden.authors: Fabien Bertillot, Solène Hervé, Zuzana Outla, Tolga Sever, Nelly Drobjazko, Mona El Gendi, Mirjam Binner, Maria O. Hernandez, Noemi Kedei, Kai Kruse, Erdogan Pekcan Erkan, Karolina Punovuori, Teijo Pellinen, Maarit Ahtiainen, Jan Böhm, Jukka-Pekka Mecklin, Markus J. Mäkinen, Caj Haglund, Jaana Hagström, NA, Mike Nikolaev, Nikolce Gjorevski, Juha P. Väyrynen, Arafath K. Najumudeen, Matthias Lütolf, Toni T. Seppälä, Sara A. Wickström, Yekaterina A. Miroshnikova
articles_hidden.abstract: Intratumoural heterogeneity, originating from genetic, epigenetic and phenotypic diversity, is pervasive in cancer and a fundamental barrier to curative treatment 1,2 . How these heterogeneous cell states emerge and co-evolve within tumours remains poorly understood. Here we develop a deep-learning framework that quantifies colorectal cancer tissue architecture and nuclear morphology at subcellular resolution to predict patient outcome. Integrating this with spatial transcriptomics, multiplex immunofluorescence and patient-derived organoids, we identify a co-evolutionary relationship between tumour architecture and cancer cell states. We identify architectural interfaces in colorectal cancer that drive cell state diversification by promoting distinct cancer stem cell programmes. Specifically, tissue fragmentation generates compressive forces that activate YAP, suppressing classical stem cell programmes and inducing fetal/regenerative stem cell states that initially manifest as hybrid states with features of partial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Subsequent tumour–stroma communication through TGFβ diversifies these into distinct stem cell and EMT states. Reciprocally, β-catenin activity tunes tumour cell responsiveness to architectural cues. Collectively, this work identifies a feedforward loop between cell states and tissue architecture that drives cancer heterogeneity and cell state diversification. Machine-learning-based analyses harness this co-dependency, independently of mutational status or cancer stage, to predict patient outcome.

articles_hidden.title: Licensing mechanisms during RNA-guided DNA integration by type I-F3 CAST
articles_hidden.authors: Shirin Fatma, Shubham Dubey, Vinh H. Truong, Seong Guk Park, Hailey M. Wallace, Alfredo Jose Florez Ariza, Isabella King, Elizabeth H. Kellogg
articles_hidden.abstract: Precise genomic integration of large DNA cargo remains a central challenge in genome engineering. CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs)1,2 offer a promising solution by coupling RNA-guided DNA recognition to transposon-mediated integration. Because of their exceptional targeting fidelity, type I-F3 CASTs have been a major research focus1, yet the structural basis of their RNA-guided DNA integration has remained unclear. Here, using cryo-electron microscopy, computational protein design and functional assays, we report the licensing mechanisms that control DNA integration activity of Vibrio cholerae CAST (VchCAST). Structural determination was enabled by zero-shot computational redesign of TnsA, which enhanced integration activity by nearly two orders of magnitude without compromising specificity. The structure of the holo integration complex reveals the conformational licensing events that govern activation of the integration machinery at the on-target site. Multiple components (Cascadeâ€“TniQ, TnsC and TnsAâ€“TnsB) undergo conformational changes upon assembly into the holo integration complex, and the catalytically competent state is stabilized only within the full assembly. Comparison with existing CAST integration complex structures reveals conserved architectural features, suggesting a common molecular basis for RNA-guided transposition across CASTs. Our findings establish a general mechanistic framework for RNA-guided DNA integration and demonstrate that protein design is a powerful strategy for engineering highly active CAST systems.

articles_hidden.title: Augmenting reality with integrated photonics
articles_hidden.authors: Zhujun Shi, Jelena Notaros, Youmin Wang, Maxwell F. Parsons, Vittal Prakasam, Nga P. Pham, Philippe Helin, Takashi Honda, Hideaki Fukuzawa, Andres Garcia Coleto, Yun Wang, Giuseppe Calafiore
articles_hidden.abstract: Augmented-reality (AR) glasses promise to transform how we interact with the world by seamlessly blending digital content with our physical surroundings. Yet making them viable for comfortable, all-day use remains deeply challenging, constrained by hard trade-offs of size, power and display performance. This calls for fundamentally new ways to generate and control light with high precision in an ultracompact form factor. Here we examine how integrated photonics can help bridge the technology gap in AR hardware. We review the basics of AR displays and recent advances in integrated photonics for new AR display components and architectures, then turn to key challenges and future directions, from component development to system innovation and scalable manufacturing, and highlight broader opportunities for synergy with fields such as quantum computing, bioimaging and optical sensing.

articles_hidden.title: Structural basis of RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CAST systems
articles_hidden.authors: Giada Finocchio, Seraina Oberli, George D. Lampe, Michael Schmitz, Samuel H. Sternberg, Martin Jinek
articles_hidden.abstract: CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) achieve site-specific DNA integration by combining the RNA-guided targeting action of a nuclease-deficient CRISPR–Cas system with the assembly of a Tn7-like transpososome complex 1,2 . Understanding the detailed mechanisms of this elaborate process is paramount to engineering CAST systems into programmable genetic tools 3–6 . Type I-F Pseudoalteromonas CAST ( Pse CAST) shows the highest activity in mammalian cells so far 7 and has been adapted extensively through directed evolution 8 . However, its continued rational engineering requires addressing critical gaps in our understanding of transpososome assembly and activation 9 . Here we perform structural analyses using cryogenic electron microscopy, validated by DNA transposition assays, to visualize the Pse CAST system in a series of functional states that define the stepwise mechanism of RNA-guided DNA integration. The structures of the Pse CAST targeting and transposase recruitment complexes revealed that conformational changes in the Cascade–TniQ module, induced by R-loop formation, are associated with target-DNA stabilization and TnsC heptamerization. This, in turn, results in the recruitment of the TnsAB transposase by conserved interactions with the carboxy-terminal tail of TnsB. Finally, the structure of the 1.2 MDa Pse CAST transpososome holocomplex revealed allosteric coupling of TnsC–TnsB and TnsB–target-DNA interactions to the conformational remodelling of the TnsB catalytic site, activating donor-DNA integration. Together, these findings establish a unified mechanistic blueprint for RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CASTs and provide a structural framework to guide their engineering for genome-editing applications.

articles_hidden.title: De novo design of high-potency dual-target therapeutic peptides with ORIDTP
articles_hidden.authors: Tianxu Lv, Bing He, Lei Guan, Yao Chen, Yiru Pu, Chenchen Qin, Fang Wang, Yuran Jia, Jiale Zhou, Yang Xiao, Yeye Guo, Nianzhou Yu, Lingling Ou, Dong Wang, Le Yang, Yang Mi, Ruoxuan Gao, Jiangning Song, Youhai H. Chen, Shilin Chen, Jun Lu, Ting Li, Jianhua Yao
articles_hidden.abstract: Peptides capable of modulating two therapeutic targets offer opportunities for treating complex diseases1,2. However, the development of such peptides at both targets is challenging, limited primarily by low design success rates and weak bioactivity. Here we present ORIDTP, an artificial intelligence platform that integrates single-target knowledge transfer and dual-target reinforcement to enable the rational design of high-potency peptides. ORIDTP successfully designed dual-target co-agonists for the GLP-1R and glucagon receptor (GCGR, also known as GLR), six of which surpassed the strongest natural binders of each receptor in bioactivity. Notably, the lead peptide GA-Dual.R5.S3 induced substantial weight loss and glycaemic improvement in diet-induced obese mice, and exhibited pronounced antidiabetic effects in db/db mice, without inducing nausea or aversion. Furthermore, ORIDTP demonstrated generalizability through successful zero-shot design of dual-target co-inhibitors for structurally and mechanistically distinct immune checkpoints, PD-1 and CTLA-4. Out of 15 designed peptides, 8 blocked both checkpoint interactions and 3 further exhibited in vivo antitumour efficacy in human checkpoint knock-in tumour-bearing mice. The lead peptide IC-Dual.P3 achieved the strongest tumour growth suppression, reducing tumour volume by 94.2% relative to controls. Together, these findings establish ORIDTP as a powerful and generalizable platform for de novo dual-target peptide discovery.

articles_hidden.title: Continuous N-to-C Peptide Synthesis
articles_hidden.authors: Jingjun Yin, Ji Qi, Zhiyan Song, Baoqiang Wan, Jin Zhang, Fangzhou Xie, Enkai Wang, Yang Cao, Hongming Li, Qixue Yuan, Jinxiang He, Xiao Wang, Liwen Xu, Chunrui Sun, Kai-Jiong Xiao, Feng Peng, Shishi Lin, Gao Shang, Lu Wang, Jing Xu, Jiwen Jiang, Xiupeng Duan, Donghong Li, Mengli Zhang, Haijiang Nan, Like Chen, Fang Wang, Tong Kang, Minyi Feng, Guiquan Liu, Louis-Charles Campeau
articles_hidden.abstract: Current state-of-the-art peptide synthesis faces a significant global challenge in efficiency and sustainability.1 With demand for peptide therapeutics growing rapidly,2,3 our ability to provide these important medicines is under increasing pressure.4 Chemical synthesis typically proceeds C-to-N and requires protecting groups, whereas ribosomal synthesis proceeds N-to-C from unprotected amino acids (AAs). To improve efficiency and sustainability, we developed a continuous N-to-C Peptide Synthesis (NCPS) using N-/C-unprotected AAs or fragments without intermediate isolations, achieving â‰¥95% average yield per coupling and â‰¤1.0% epimerization. The method enabled seven consecutive couplings. Starting from N-/C-unprotected AAs, peptide assembly requires fewer isolations than those needed to prepare the corresponding Fmoc-AA building blocks before conventional synthesis can begin. This method accepts all 20 canonical AAs and a wide range of non-canonical AAs important for drug-like profiles.5 Longer peptides can be readily assembled through continuous fragment coupling while maintaining chiral integrity. This approach reduces isolations by ~10-fold and waste generation by up to ~100-fold. We further developed a flow synthesizer that enhances speed and productivity while mitigating batch manufacturing risks. The method enabled the synthesis of a tirzepatide heptapeptide fragment, degarelix, a 14-mer engineered macrocyclic peptide, and semaglutide. Overall, continuous NCPS has the potential to transform peptide manufacturing.

articles_hidden.title: Hexa-substituted benzene synthesis with non-classical carbocations
articles_hidden.authors: Guillaume Mollaert, Hang-Fei Tu, Jacob R. King, Mihai V. Popescu, Zexian Li, Quan Zhang, Eric Palomo, Robert S. Paton, Marcos G. Suero
articles_hidden.abstract: Benzene rings are the most frequently encountered ring system in small-molecule drugs1. However, benzenes with six substituents are notably absent from small molecule libraries, owing to challenges associated with their synthesis and the limited availability of commercially available aromatic building blocks2. Therefore, new chemical processes that enable their synthesis with predictable regiochemical control and broad substituent diversity could enable medicinal chemists to explore this uncharted aromatic chemical space in hit-to-lead and lead optimization campaigns. Herein, we describe a highly modular and programmable platform for accessing hexa-substituted benzene rings from aromatic cyclopropenium cations and (trialkylsilyl)allenes, with precise control over all six benzene positions encoded in the starting materials. The exceptional regioselectivity observed originates from the selective evolution of an unusual non-classical carbocation featuring four-centre four-electron bonding as revealed by density functional theory calculations. Our benzannulation enables the selective installation of synthetic handles that were exploited for the synthesis of previously inaccessible penta- and hexa-substituted analogues of the anticancer drug sonidegib and the antihypertensive drug telmisartan, as well as the polyaromatic hydrocarbon triphenylene. Notably, the use of enantiopure allenes unlocks a new route to enantioenriched multi-substituted biaryls through our benzannulation occurring with â€œmemory of chiralityâ€.

articles_hidden.title: Architecture of the poxvirus early-transcription machinery and portal complex
articles_hidden.authors: Benoît Arragain, Lukas W. Bauer, Victor-Valentin Hodirnau, Florian K. M. Schur
articles_hidden.abstract: Poxviruses enclose a complete viral transcription machinery alongside their dsDNA genome within the viral core, a transcription-competent compartment delimited by a permeable multi-layered protein shell. Upon infection of a cell and core release, this machinery almost immediately starts synthesizing early mRNAs, which are extruded across the core wall into the cytoplasm for translation. While in vitro structures of the isolated viral DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (vRNAP) have been described1â€“3, its native in virio architecture, spatial organization, and physical coupling to the genome remain unknown. Using cryo-electron tomography and sub-tomogram averaging on purified Vaccinia virus cores, we reveal that packaged vRNAP exists not as monomer, but as massive 1.8 MDa resting-state dimer bridged by fully ordered vaccinia virus early transcription factor (VETF). We also identify a subpopulation of these dimers bound to the essential kinase VPK2 and the core protein L4, which directly tether the transcribing engines to the packaged genome near the inner core wall. Furthermore, we determine a sub-nanometer structure of the putative poxvirus mRNA extrusion portal complex, revealing a rigid assembly integrated into the core wall comprising an E8 hexameric crown, an E6 hexameric central hub, and a basal L3 dodecameric channel suited for nucleic acid export. Together, these structures provide a comprehensive architectural blueprint of important components of the poxvirus core and open new structural and functional avenues for investigating poxvirus genome packaging, transcription activation, and mRNA extrusion.

articles_hidden.title: Submillimetre hot-electron transport in manganese-doped quantum dot solids
articles_hidden.authors: Whi Dong Kim, Clément Livache, Ho Jin, Valerio Pinchetti, Tung H. Dang, Oleg V. Kozlov, Heeyoung Jung, Zachary L. Robinson, Victor I. Klimov
articles_hidden.abstract: Colloidal quantum dot solids are promising for photoconversion and photochemistry, but their performance is fundamentally limited by rapid hot-carrier cooling, low carrier mobility and short transport ranges1. Here we demonstrate a spin-exchange-driven phototransport regime in manganese-doped quantum dot films that enables the generation, long-range transport and regeneration of hot carriers. Ultrafast spin-exchange-mediated Auger upconversion promotes electrons into high-energy, delocalized states before phonon cooling2,3, establishing a transient high-mobility conduction channel. Crucially, spin-exchange interactions not only generate hot carriers but also enable their repeated re-excitation, thereby sustaining long-range drift. This mechanism yields room-temperature mobilities of about 150â€‰cm2â€‰Vâˆ’1â€‰sâˆ’1 and submillimetre drift lengthsâ€”far greater than those of conventional quantum dot solids and approaching values characteristic of crystalline semiconductors. Time-of-flight measurements confirm drift-dominated transport, with transit times scaling linearly with distance and inversely with electric field. These results establish a route to long-range energy transport in nanoscale materials and enable the use of hot carriers in photoconversion, photochemistry and transit-time-limited photodetection.

articles_hidden.title: An in situ redox-converted molecule for all-perovskite tandem solar cells
articles_hidden.authors: Shaomin Yang, Chunxiang Lan, Miaomiao Zeng, Liqing Wu, Tian Zhang, Mimi Fu, Boyu Yang, Ziwei Zheng, Yu Wu, Jing Guo, Rui Guo, Mi Xu, Rongyan Wen, Zaiwei Wang, Shuangyan Hu, Mostafa Boshta, Jun Chen, Yaoguang Rong, Xiong Li
articles_hidden.abstract: All-perovskite tandem solar cells (TSCs) are gaining prominence due to their ability to surpass the efficiency limit of single-junction perovskite solar cells (PSCs)1,2. However, the efficiency and stability of all-perovskite TSCs are limited by chemical instability at the hole transport layer/perovskite interface in the tin-lead (Sn-Pb) narrow-bandgap subcell, which introduces deep trap states from tin cations and promotes non-radiative recombination3-5. Here we incorporate a redox-converted molecule of p-aminobenzohydrazide (ABH) into poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) that neutralizes PSS acidity, heals Sn4+ defects, and generates a dipole passivation effect upon oxidation. During the preparation of Sn-Pb perovskites, ABH suppresses interfacial oxidation by reducing Sn4+ defects and converts toÂ p-aminobenzaldehyde (ABD), which suppresses photogenerated hole-induced Sn2+ oxidation, aligning energy levels for efficient hole extraction. The in situ redox-converted molecule stabilizes the buried interface during both device fabrication and operation, reduces non-radiative recombination and enhances stability. The resulting narrow-bandgap Sn-Pb PSC achieves a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 25.4% (certified 25.2%) with an open-circuit voltage of 0.92 V and a fill factor of 83.4%. Integrated into monolithic all-perovskite TSCs, the device delivers a PCE of 31.1% (certified 30.8%) together with enhanced thermal (ISOS-D-2I, 85 Â°C) and operational stability (ISOS-L-1I) under inert conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts
articles_hidden.authors: Jianmin Wang, Jonathan A. Knott, Grant M. Domke, Brady S. Hardiman, Brian F. Walters, Songlin Fei
articles_hidden.abstract: Climate change and disturbances are reshaping forest ecosystems worldwide 1–4 , yet their combined effects on species redistribution remain poorly understood. Here we analyse repeated measurements from 44,368 forest inventory plots spanning 1999–2025, with an average remeasurement interval of 10 years, to examine how climate and natural disturbances jointly influence the elevational redistribution of tree species across the western USA. We show that climate warming increased sapling abundance, whereas increasing drought frequency and recent natural disturbances (fire, insect outbreaks and disease) reduced tree abundance, particularly among adult trees. By contrast, legacy fire was associated with increased sapling abundance, with stronger positive responses in angiosperms than in gymnosperms. These influences were distributed unevenly across species’ elevational ranges: upper portions of species’ ranges generally experienced stronger warming, greater increases in drought frequency and more disturbance activity than lower portions, creating elevational asymmetries in stress and recovery. These elevational asymmetries were associated with more pronounced downslope shifts in basal area centres, probably reflecting disturbance effects on larger trees. By contrast, stem abundance centres showed more divergent shifts, consistent with sapling responses to both climate change and disturbance. Our findings reveal contrasting demographic responses to climate change and natural disturbances that shape the elevational redistribution of different species, with potential consequences for forest composition, resilience and long-term stability.

articles_hidden.title: Transcription from megabase-scale heterochromatin generates neural barcodes
articles_hidden.authors: Alex Buckley, Carlo Vetralla, Brendan Rose, Jash Gada, Gabrielle Servito, Antonina Hafner, Sedona Murphy, Michael Mui, Alistair Nicol Boettiger, Daniele Canzio
articles_hidden.abstract: Heterochromatin typically represses genes 1,2 , yet some genes paradoxically require it for activation 3–7 . How can the same chromatin environment both silence and promote transcription? Here we address this question by interrogating the clustered protocadherin (Pcdh) locus, where subsets of genes are stochastically expressed while most remain silent 8 . In neurons, stochastic and combinatorial expression of Pcdh genes generates unique cell-surface barcodes required for self–non-self discrimination and neural circuit assembly 8 . By combining RNA labelling of Pcdh genes and neurodevelopmental cell types with single-molecule chromatin tracing and stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy, we find that a compact heterochromatin domain containing Pcdh genes forms as these genes become activated during development. Pcdh transcription occurs within the compact domain and reads through downstream genes, and distal enhancers must access the domain to engage target promoters. Genetic perturbations in mice suggest that opposing genome folding forces cooperate to establish Pcdh locus architecture and promote stochastic Pcdh expression. Specifically, while DNA loop extrusion allows enhancers to breach heterochromatin and find target promoters, heterochromatin-driven compartmentalization supports an expanded enhancer–promoter search space. These findings shed light on a process foundational to the development of vertebrate nervous systems and suggest a mechanism for how transcription can occur within seemingly silent chromatin environments.

articles_hidden.abstract: Highly heritable, polygenic and easily measured, adult height has long been the model trait in human genetics1,2. Although the landscape of height-associated common genetic variation has been studied extensively2, rare variation remains relatively unexplored1. Here, using rare protein-altering variants in a discovery set of 826,066 exomes, we identify 207 height-associated genes, 98% of which replicate in an additional 624,567 individuals. The rarest and most deleterious class of variation, singleton (frequencyâ€‰<â€‰0.0001%) putative loss-of-function variants, implicated 17 genes with large effects on height ranging from âˆ’17cm (ACAN) to +11â€‰cm (FBN1) per allele, 52Ã— larger than the average effect of common height-associated variants and comparable to the 1% tails of a common variant polygenic score. Several genes (TET1, DTL and IGF2BP2) have effect sizes that are at least as large as established Mendelian height genes, yet lack documented stature or skeletal growth syndromes, particularly for genes associated with increased height. Our large-scale sequencing study elucidates the genetic architecture and allelic heterogeneity of rare variantsÂ in height, providing unique insights into their large effectsâ€”often similar to or larger than recognized Mendelian syndromesâ€”and their impact on trait prediction, clinical evaluation, and discovery power to facilitate drug target prioritization.

articles_hidden.title: Enzymatic living polymerization for polysaccharide synthesis
articles_hidden.authors: Lin Yin, Qi He, Yingxin Wang, Xinyu Bian, Xiaoduo Dong, Yating Liu, Shanshan Li, Xiangyun Xu, Jieyi An, Xiangcheng Pan, Myongsoo Lee, Long Li, Guosong Chen
articles_hidden.abstract: Polysaccharides have myriad functions throughout biological processes, yet synthetic access to well-defined analogues remains a challenge1,2. Achieving high molecular weight, controlled stereochemistry and sequence precision simultaneously has been elusive using conventional chemical methods that rely on protecting-group manipulations. Here we propose enzymatic living polymerization, which enables the precision preparation of natural polysaccharides with molecular weights up to 660â€‰kgâ€‰molâˆ’1 but polydispersity from low to less than 1.05. Such a living behaviour originates from the initiator weakly binding with the polymerase, realizing fast equilibrium of the active (bound) and dormant (unbound) species, as demonstrated by mechanistic and computational studies. Our approach is generalizable to diverse polysaccharide types, including sequence-controlled block copolymers, and provides a modular route to explore molecular-weight-dependent biological functions of natural polysaccharides.

articles_hidden.abstract: Modern and future electronics harbour a key challenge: as conventional metal wires shrink to nanoscale dimensions, their resistivity increases sharply1 owing to surface and grain-boundary scattering. To circumvent this unwanted behaviour, here,Â we explore the fundamental limits of charge transport in topological semimetal niobium phosphide (NbP) nanoribbons down to approximately 6-nm widths, with industry-friendly top-down nanofabrication. The extracted NbP nanoribbon resistivity reaches 18â€‰Â±â€‰4.1â€‰Î¼Î©â€‰cm at room temperature with an approximately 9-nm2 cross-sectional area, lower than that of conventional metals and semimetals with comparable size. The NbP nanoribbon resistivity decreases with decreasing width, unlike the classical behaviour of metals such as copper. This trend suggests a growing relative contribution of surface and edge states as the nanoribbon cross-section is reduced, despite a certain amount of disorder, including edge roughness. Our findings advance the understanding of size-dependent transport and scaling in this class of semimetals, offering a platform for nanoscale wires and interconnects in future nanoelectronics.

articles_hidden.title: Sustainable cement production via a liquid-phase pathway
articles_hidden.authors: Qi Zheng, Haiyan Mao, Chengyao Liang, Xinyu Dou, Stuart McElhany, Cruz Carlos, Xiaohong Zhu, Jiawei Wang, Yuqi Li, Xiwen Chi, Dilworth Parkinson, Roya Maboudian, Peter Ercius, Robert B. Jackson, Yi Cui, Paulo J. M. Monteiro
articles_hidden.abstract: Slowing climate change requires overcoming inertia in political, technological and geophysical systems1,2,3. Portland cement manufacturing is among the most challenging industrial processes to decarbonize, yet it remains indispensable for building the infrastructure underpinning the low-carbon transition4,5. Here, building beyond the two-century-old conventional cement process6, we report a route that creates sustainable cement, by accelerating its reaction kinetics through a microwave carbon-plasma method, reducing the standard processing time from hours to seconds. Our technique generates localized temperatures up to 2,400â€‰Â°C, sufficient to liquefy the raw materials. These liquid-phase reactions promote elemental mixing and solidification, producing reactive clinker phases. Our in situ transmission electron microscopy captures the early-stage cement hydration process in real time, revealing that surface disorder accelerates clinkerÂ reactivity by facilitating the dynamic nucleation and growth of hydration clusters. Beyond typical limestone and clay feedstocks, we show that hydrated cement paste from waste concrete can also be processed into clinkers, meeting ordinary Portland cement specifications. By coupling circular resource use with ultrafast electrified processing, our approach enables sustainable, low-cost cement production at scale.

articles_hidden.authors: Helena Sabata, Ariadna Roca-Coll, Jose A. Castillo, Nathalie Tisch, Macarena De Andrés-Laguillo, Sophie Payne, Judith Llena, Svanhild Nornes, Pilar Villacampa, Dorota Szumska, Ana Rita Grosso, Karina Yaniv, Bart Vanhaesebroeck, María P. Alcolea, Sarah De Val, Susana Lopez-Fernandez, Katrien De Bock, Eulalia Baselga, Rui Benedito, Michael Potente, Ana Angulo-Urarte, Mariona Graupera
articles_hidden.abstract: Cancer-associated mutations in PIK3CA underlie congenital overgrowth disorders that frequently involve the vasculature1,2. Among the affected tissues, the endothelium commonly exhibits aberrant expansion, leading to vascular malformations3. Notably, these lesions arise predominantly in veins and capillaries, whereas arteries are largely spared, for reasons that remain unclear. Here, using genetic lineage tracing, we show that endothelial expression of PIK3CAH1047R drives profound clonal expansion of capillary and venous endothelial cells, whereas mature arterial endothelial cells are refractory to pathological PI3K activation. Expression of PIK3CAH1047R in arterial precursors disrupts arterial differentiation and promotes the acquisition of venous features, providing a mechanistic explanation for the paucity of arterial lesions after PIK3CA genetic perturbation. Mechanistically, these effects are mediated by two complementary downstream branches of PI3K signalling: increased proliferation, which drives vascular overgrowth, and upregulation of the venous-specifying transcription factor NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), which suppresses arterial differentiation. Together, our findings reveal that pathogenic responses to PIK3CAH1047R are dictated by endothelial differentiation state and fate trajectory, and demonstrate that arterial endothelium is intrinsically resistant to oncogenic PI3K signalling. Arteries are therefore shielded from PIK3CA mutations, explaining the rarity of arterial malformations in PIK3CA-driven disease.

articles_hidden.title: An extremophile transgene improves drought resistance and yield in cereals
articles_hidden.authors: Linying Du, Fangfang Li, Xu Qian, Hongqing Zhu, Chunhao Fang, Chen Wang, Zhen Qin, Bingbing Li, Suxin Wang, Ping Jiang, Yuting Hou, Xueling Huang, Dongling Tang, Bin Chen, Shiqi Yang, Qiannan Wang, Shijie Tian, Zhangtong Sun, Liangliang Song, Ming Yu, Tongfang Xing, Yuling Liu, Shuangxing Zhang, Peiyin Zhang, Wenxuan Feng, Jin Hu, Jing Zhao, Gangming Zhan, Shumin Li, Yanyan Wang, Jiangchun Wei, Zhensheng Kang, Hude Mao
articles_hidden.abstract: Drought is a major environmental constraint limiting global crop production1,2. On average, crop productivity typically declines by 30â€“40% in moderate-drought years, whereas extreme droughts trigger far greater reductions3,4. As droughts become longer and more intense due to climate change, adverse effects on crop productivity are expected to escalate5. Breaking the trade-offs between stress resistance and yield is key to advancing crop genetic improvement as climate change sets in and the world population grows, but this is challenging for drought stress6. Here we show that heterologous expression of EpTFIIAÎ³, a gene encoding a transcription factor induced by osmotic stress in an extremophile lichen mycobiont, partially decouples trade-offs between stress resistance and grain production, enhancing plot yields of five wheat cultivars under water deficit by 19.4â€“32.8%, and per-plant yields of rice and maize by 19.7â€“42.4% in the greenhouse and multiple field environments. EpTFIIAÎ³ physically interacts with endogenous transcriptional activators to synergistically enhance both stress-responsive and developmental transcriptional programs, simultaneously boosting photosynthetic capacity and water-use efficiency, while delaying senescence via multiple physiological and developmental enhancements, ultimately increasing grain yields. EpTFIIAÎ³ uncouples antagonistic stress-response and biomass production pathways in multiple crops and delivers a straightforwards and broad-spectrum strategy for sustainably improving staple-crop yields regardless of water availability.

articles_hidden.abstract: Quantum metrology promises measurement precision beyond classical limits by exploiting large-scale quantum states1,2,3,4,5,6,7, yet realizing this advantage faces two fundamental challenges: the deterministic preparation of non-trivial quantum probes8,9 and the efficient extraction of metrological information in high-dimensional Hilbert spaces10,11,12. Here, we introduce quantum confocal microscopy in Fock space that addresses these challenges for a Fock-like probe state with a tightly concentrated photon-number distribution. Drawing a direct analogy between classical wave optics and quantum state evolution in a bosonic mode13,14, we construct a confocal lens system with a quantum circuit of \({\mathcal{O}}(1)\) operational depth, realizing a bidirectional transformation between a readily obtainable coherent state and this Fock-like probe state. Using a superconducting circuit quantum electrodynamics platform, we deterministically prepare focused probe states with mean photon numbers up to NÂ =Â 500, achieving a 21.5Â Â±Â 1.1â€‰dB reduction of the photon-number variance relative to a coherent state. Using the focused states for displacement sensing, we achieve a record metrological gain of 19.20Â Â±Â 0.20â€‰dB beyond the standard quantum limit. This work establishes quantum confocal microscopy as a compact protocol that makes high-photon-number non-Gaussian Fock-like probes experimentally accessible and measurable, providing a viable route towards quantum-enhanced precision measurement, and is readily extendable to other bosonic platforms and high-dimensional quantum many-body systems.

Empirical evidence for eight ways that AI is impacting people
articles.authors: Christopher Summerfield, Rebecca Anselmetti, Shahar Avin, Vanessa Cheung, Madga Dubois, Tom Eccles, Anna Gausen, Kobi Hackenburg, Keno Juechems, Hannah Rose Kirk, Lennart Luettgau, Brendan McGrath, Ishan Mishra, Aidan Peppin, Jorge Perez, Nadine Staes-Polet, Merlin Stein, Andrew Strait, Sarenne Wallbridge
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are now used by one billion people worldwide. What is their impact on human users? Popular narratives of concern argue that AI may be undermining our cognitive abilities, polluting our information ecosystem, corroding human relationships, damaging our mental health and rendering us vulnerable to persuasion, manipulation, emotional dependence and social engineering. Does the empirical evidence support these claims? Emerging research has begun to study the impact that AI has on people, via model evaluations, user studies, analysis of consumer chatlogs and agent-based simulations. Here we review this evidence, finding limited evidence for the strongest narratives of concern. However, research is still nascent and many uncertainties remain to be resolved in future work.

articles.abstract: A carbon price is an effective and cost-efficient policy to mitigate emissions, yet low public acceptance and limited political support remain major barriers to its widespread implementation. This crowdsourced ‘many-designs’ project presents results from 55 behavioural interventions on real-world support for carbon pricing, independently developed by international research teams. By implementing all designs simultaneously with almost 20,000 US residents, this preregistered study shows very small positive but statistically significant effects of behavioural interventions on a set of design-specific proxies of real-world support (Cohen’s d = 0.06; 99.5% confidence interval (CI) 0.001 to 0.124) and on 4 out of 5 common measures of stated support (Cohen’s d values 0.06–0.08; 99.5% CIs from 0.006 to 0.112 and from 0.020 to 0.133; between 1.7 and 2.4 percentage points in increased support across outcomes), including the willingness to endorse a carbon price that internalizes the social costs of US$120 per ton of CO 2 emissions ( d = 0.06; 99.5% CI 0.012 to 0.118). Furthermore, the results reveal low-to-medium between-study heterogeneity ( τ = 0.07–0.12). Lastly, we identify strong overconfidence among research teams regarding the expected effects of their interventions and those of their peers, indicating a miscalibration of community expectations.

articles_hidden.title: Multidimensional motor unit control after paralysing spinal cord injury using non-invasive recordings
articles_hidden.authors: Xingchen Yang, Vishal Rawji, Ciara Gibbs, Tianyu Jia, Lara Gouveia Vila, Agnese Grison, Ajoy Nair, Dario Farina, Juan Alvaro Gallego
articles_hidden.abstract: Spinal cord injury results in profound motor impairment, which affects approximately 20 million people worldwide. Regaining hand use is one of their highest priorities. Interestingly, even severely affected individuals can still use spared connections to generate detectable activity (measured with electromyography) in their paralysed muscles when attempting to perform a movement. Here we asked whether participants with no hand function due to a cervical spinal cord injury could still control the activity of motor units from paralysed muscles, which we detected using high-density surface electromyographic recordings. Participants could readily control their motor units to accurately perform three different one-dimensional tracking tasks that imposed different control requirements, with performance plateauing after a few days of practice. Moreover, this accurate control readily transferred to a two-dimensional cursor navigation task, allowing participants to play a series of one-dimensional (‘Pong’) and two-dimensional (‘Snake’) games and to navigate a virtual wheelchair using three independent control signals. This robust performance was achieved despite the presence of spasticity, and even in one participant who had a motor complete injury. These findings demonstrate the promise of non-invasive motor unit recordings for restoring hand function and suggest potential avenues for rehabilitation after paralysis.

articles_hidden.title: Linguistic contextualization in the human hippocampus
articles_hidden.authors: Kalman A. Katlowitz, James L. Belanger, Taha Ismail, Ana G. Chavez, Assia Chericoni, Melissa Franch, Elizabeth A. Mickiewicz, Raissa K. Mathura, Alica M. Goldman, Vaishnav Krishnan, Atul Maheshwari, Mohammed Hasen, Danika L. Paulo, Andrew J. Watrous, Eleonora Bartoli, Steven T. Piantadosi, Nicole R. Provenza, Sameer A. Sheth, Benjamin Y. Hayden
articles_hidden.abstract: Word meanings in language are contextualized by surrounding words. Inspired by the self-attention mechanism in transformer-based large language models (LLMs), we hypothesized that structural composition in the brain arises from combining canonical (non-contextual) word representations with those of nearby words. We analysed single unit activity in the human hippocampus, a region involved in semantic and contextual processing, while nâ€‰=â€‰10 participants listened to podcasts. We found that hippocampal neurons encoded word position within a clause, using both ordinal and frequency-domain positional encoding. Moreover, neural responses to specific words reflected both the lexical semantics of the word and a weighted sum of the embeddings of preceding words. The relative weighting of these contextualizing words correlated with LLM self-attention weights. These findings suggest that contextualization in the brain makes use of vectorial shifts that have a resemblance to attentional reweighting in LLMs, and highlight the role of the mesial temporal lobe within the broader language network.

articles.title: Reducing belief in conspiracy theories as they unfold using large language models
articles.authors: Thomas H. Costello, Nathaniel Rabb, Michael Nicholas Stagnaro, Gordon Pennycook, David G. Rand
articles.abstract: The emergence of conspiracy theories in the wake of major events is a significant societal challenge. Here, we test whether conversational dialogues with a large language model (LLM) can reduce belief in immediately unfolding conspiracies. In experiments conducted in the days following the July 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump and the September 2025 assassination of Charlie Kirk, US adults (Experiment 1: N = 472; Experiment 2: N = 1,042) holding conspiratorial views about the crisis event engaged in a multiturn conversation with an LLM prompted to reduce their conspiracy belief. Compared to control participants who either discussed an irrelevant topic with an LLM or viewed a static fact sheet, participants in the LLM treatment showed significantly reduced conspiracy beliefs in both experiments. We also found suggestive evidence of downstream effects of the LLM treatment, observing reduced belief in some—but not all—analyses of different conspiratorial beliefs 1 to 2 mo later. These results shed light on the psychology of emerging conspiracies and highlight the potential for scalable, information-focused LLM interventions to counteract misinformation in the immediate aftermath of high-profile societal events.

articles.title: Promises and pitfalls of community moderation on social media
articles.authors: Isabelle Augenstein, Michiel A. Bakker, Tanmoy Chakraborty, David Corney, Emilio Ferrara, Iryna Gurevych, Scott Hale, Eduard Hovy, Heng Ji, Irene Larraz, Filippo Menczer, Preslav Nakov, Paolo Papotti, Dhruv Sahnan, Greta Warren, Giovanni Zagni
articles.abstract: Social media platforms have traditionally relied on internal moderation teams and partnerships with independent fact-checking organizations to identify and flag problematic content. Recently, however, platforms including X (formerly Twitter) and Meta have shifted toward community-driven content moderation by launching their own versions of crowd-sourced fact-checking—Community Notes. If effectively scaled and governed, such crowd-checking initiatives have the potential to combat misinformation as successfully as community-driven efforts once did with spam. However, moderating misinformation is inherently more complex: perceptions of truth are often shaped by personal biases, political leanings, and cultural contexts, complicating consensus on what constitutes misleading content. This suggests that community efforts, while valuable, cannot replace the indispensable role of professional fact-checkers. Here we explore the emerging role of community-driven moderation, critically evaluate both the promises and the challenges of Community Notes at scale, and identify how collaborative and technical innovations can integrate the two distinct approaches.

articles.title: Sea-fishing cultures show rare blend of tight social ties and openness to strangers
articles.abstract: Research has linked cultural differences to historical subsistence styles, but most studies have focused on farming or herding. Sea fishing is a major subsistence style, yet we know much less about whether fishing shapes culture. We propose an explanation for why fishing has received less attention—its cultural patterns do not fit neatly into the individualism-collectivism dichotomy that has been so useful in studies of farming and herding. First, we tested 1,010 people from nearby regions in Japan as a more controlled comparison. Then we tested the generalizability of the findings across 150 contemporary nations and historical records from 1,265 ethnic groups worldwide. People from fishing regions think holistically and emphasize responsibilities in close relationships more than people in nonfishing cultures (culture level d = 0.91). These characteristics are more common in collectivistic cultures and may have been adaptive for cooperation in dangerous seas. However, they show less ingroup loyalty and less outgroup discrimination ( d = 1.37), which is more similar to individualistic cultures. Openness to outsiders may have been adaptive for fishing’s mobility and flexible labor networks. We address reverse causality by running instrumental variable analyses using data on environmental suitability for fishing. To pinpoint fishing, we compare regions that have coastlines, some by seas that support large fish populations and others that support few fish. Results show access to the ocean, trade, or transportation are not linked to these cultural differences. Finally, the cultural patterns do not extend to freshwater fishing, which has different demands from sea fishing.

articles.title: Humans show limited ability to distinguish human-authored from AI-generated political content on social media
articles.authors: Sejin Paik, Tiago Ventura, Rebecca Ansell, Leticia Bode, Autumn Toney-Wails, Lisa Singh
articles.abstract: This study employs a set of behavioral experiments to examine how individuals perceive the humanness of social media posts about the 2024 U.S. presidential debate between Kamala Harris and Donald Trump. Posts presented in the experiment were authored either by humans or chatbots, varying the large language model (LLM), the model architecture, the social media platform, and the political personas. Participants judged randomly paired posts to identify which they perceived to be AI-generated. We find that human-authored posts were on average perceived as more human-like than AI outputs generated from five of the six LLMs in this study. However, participants’ ability to detect AI-generated content is limited. They do so only slightly above chance in human–AI pairs, and this ability weakens for newer LLMs, varies by platform, and reflects partisan bias. Only posts generated with Llama 3.3 scored, on average, higher on perceived humanness than human-authored posts. The social media platform also mattered, with participants distinguishing human from AI on most platforms (YouTube, TikTok, Truth Social), but not on X/Twitter. Incivility and negative emotions are associated with high humanness perceptions, and partisan identity also shaped evaluations, with Republican respondents more likely to view ideologically misaligned AI posts as AI-generated.

articles.title: Cognitive diversity and majority rule
articles.authors: Lu Hong, P. J. Lamberson, Scott E. Page, Ville A. Satopää
articles.abstract: Societies rely on groups–boards, panels, committees, and representative bodies–to make important decisions for good reason: overwhelming evidence shows groups usually make more accurate choices than individuals. The predominant logic for group accuracy rests on reasoning formulated in the Condorcet Jury Theorem, which states that if voters receive independent and equally accurate generated signals, majority rule produces decisions that i) are more accurate than the average voter, ii) improve in individual accuracy and iii) group size, and iv) approach perfect accuracy as group size becomes large. An alternative logic based on interpreted signals explains the accuracy of majority rule as arising from the aggregation of diverse mental models. Group accuracy results from the same state of the world being classified differently by different people. In this framework, the set of possible group accuracies can be characterized conditional on average individual accuracy and average pairwise diversity. Majority rule groups are only guaranteed to outperform their members when diversity is high. Using data from a variety of empirical settings, along with simulations of a minimal nearest-neighbor model, we find much stronger support for the predictions of the interpreted signals framework than for the standard generated signals model. We further show empirical evidence for a diversity–accuracy paradox, in which more diverse groups are less accurate unless average individual accuracy is nearly constant across groups. Our findings have important implications for group composition and institutional and organizational design as well as for the potential gains from deliberation.

articles_hidden.title: A herbivore-induced plant volatile facilitates group foraging in locusts
articles_hidden.authors: Lingzhi Shi, Jinmeng Guo, Jinxi Yuan, Yan Yan, Jiancai Li, Guirong Wang, Bill S. Hansson, Hetan Chang
articles_hidden.abstract: Plants have evolved sophisticated defense strategies against herbivory, often releasing volatile compounds upon attack to deter further feeding. Here, we demonstrate the induced volatile S-linalool promotes phase- and stage-specific group foraging in the migratory locust ( Locusta migratoria ). We show that S-linalool, a volatile whose emission increases more than 10-fold following damage by gregarious nymphs, acts as a potent attractant that drives other nymphs to aggregate and feed on previously attacked rice plants. Mechanistically, we identified the olfactory receptor LmOR49 that detects S-linalool and used genome editing to make this receptor nonfunctional, thereby abolishing both electrophysiological responses and behavioral attraction. We also inactivated rice genes required for S-linalool biosynthesis, abolishing its emission, rendering plants unattractive, and disrupting locust feeding preference. Although feeding on previously attacked plants provides no detectable direct fitness benefit under our experimental conditions, prior locust feeding suppresses the accumulation of deterrent metabolites, potentially increasing plant palatability for subsequent feeding. S-linalool thus serves as an olfactory cue that guides gregarious nymphs toward previously attacked, more palatable plants. Collectively, these findings uncover a comprehensive mechanism whereby a plant defense volatile is exploited by an insect herbivore to promote group foraging, broadening our understanding of plant–insect interactions and suggesting molecular targets for locust control.

articles_hidden.title: Quantifying (de)mixing of disordered proteins in molecular dynamics simulations
articles_hidden.authors: William Morton, Robert Vácha
articles_hidden.abstract: Biomolecular condensates control the spatial and temporal organization of cellular biochemistry. Their architectures often arise from complex, multicomponent mixtures governed by weak, multivalent interactions between intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins. However, current approaches lack generalizable metrics to determine whether IDRs will mix or segregate within condensates. Here, we present a domain decomposition method (DDM) that accurately determines phase concentrations without identifying condensate interfaces. When tested against 399 IDR simulations, the DDM recovers dense- and dilute-phase concentrations within 1% agreement of established surface-based methods. By calculating spatial variances to map three-dimensional organization, this approach successfully distinguishes homogeneous mixing from surface enrichment, core–shell architectures, and complete segregation. Applying this continuous metric to 2,068 binary mixtures of 32 distinct IDRs, we demonstrate that physicochemical similarity strongly promotes mixing. Hydrophobic IDRs mixed promiscuously across all partner chemistries, whereas charged sequences mixed in a way highly sensitive to charge complementarity, forming the most stable condensates as net charge approached zero. Compared with experimental networks, our IDR-only simulations predicted the partitioning preferences for 10 of 13 proteins, with discrepancies accurately isolating cases where colocalization strictly requires RNA or folded domains. Quantifying mixing in this way provides a robust and reproducible method for predicting IDR interactomes and understanding the composition of complex cellular condensates.

articles_hidden.title: Inactivation of the RB1 and PTPN14 tumor suppressors cooperatively enables the lifespan extension activity of the human papillomavirus E7 oncoprotein
articles_hidden.authors: Pushkal Sinduvadi Ramesh, Angelo A. Nicolaci, Leah E. Graham, Joangela Nouel, Kevin Xu, Jennifer M. Binning, Karl Munger, Elizabeth A. White
articles_hidden.abstract: High-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) E7 proteins bind and inactivate host cellular tumor suppressors and are essential for the immortalization of primary human keratinocytes. E7 proteins from high- and low-risk HPV genotypes bind directly to at least two tumor suppressors, RB1 and PTPN14, and inactivate both. We previously characterized mutations in high-risk HPV E7 proteins that selectively abrogate the ability of E7 to bind either RB1 or PTPN14. Here, we established a genetic complementation system using the E7 mutants defective for binding to RB1 or PTPN14. Neither mutant alone could extend the lifespan of primary keratinocytes. When expressed together, the mutants could, like wild-type high-risk HPV E7, extend keratinocyte lifespan. Both high- and low-risk E7 reduced PTPN14 protein levels and reduced expression of keratinocyte differentiation genes, whereas only high-risk E7 reduced steady-state RB1 levels and induced E2F-dependent genes. Depletion of either RB1 or PTPN14 could cooperate with low-risk HPV6 E7 to extend keratinocyte lifespan. Our findings advance the model that inactivation of at least two tumor suppressors is required for the lifespan extension activity of high-risk HPV E7.

articles_hidden.title: Anterior cingulate cortex neurons parse speakers in a natural cocktail party
articles_hidden.authors: Arthur Lefevre, Vikram Pal Singh, Timothy J. Tyree, Jingwen Li, Pia Giraudet, Jean-René Duhamel, Cory T. Miller
articles_hidden.abstract: The cocktail party problem—parsing relevant voices from competing speakers—has traditionally been studied as a sensory challenge for auditory cortex. Yet in natural communication, identifying speakers and coordinating interaction are inherently social processes. Here we recorded single neurons from anterior cingulate cortex (ACC, area 24) in freely moving marmosets engaged in spontaneous vocal exchanges within a noisy colony environment. ACC neurons selectively encoded vocalizations from a social partner versus other callers in the scene, effectively parsing speakers in the acoustic mixture. This selectivity was preserved even when vocalizations overlapped in time, indicating robustness to background interference. Apart from perception, ACC population activity represented vocal production, call type, and whether calls occurred within vocal turn-taking exchanges. Behaviorally, marmosets adjusted vocal timing based on the surrounding acoustic scene, and these interaction contexts were reliably reflected in ACC activity. Together, these findings suggest that neurons in ACC play a role in parsing conspecific speakers during communication in a natural “cocktail party,” linking auditory scene analysis with social monitoring and coordinated interactions.

articles_hidden.title: Influence of noninertial dynamics on static quantum resource theories
articles_hidden.authors: Saveetha Harikrishnan, Tim Byrnes, Chandrashekar Radhakrishnan
articles_hidden.abstract: The effect of noninertial dynamics on static quantum resource theories is investigated. To this end, we first show the equivalence between noninertial effects and a completely positive, trace-preserving (CPTP) map. In this formulation, the Unruh effect is equivalent to a bosonic amplifier channel. The effect of this map on a generic quantum resource is investigated by studying the role of the CPTP map on the three core ingredients of a resource theory, namely, the free states, the free operations, and the resource quantifiers. We show several general statements can be made about these three components of a resource theory in the presence of noninertial motion.

articles_hidden.title: Rethinking broad diet breadth as a sign of scarcity: A 50,000-y record of subsistence from northwestern Australia
articles_hidden.authors: Tiina Manne, Erin Mein, Jane Balme, Sue O’Connor, Ken Aplin, Peter Veth
articles_hidden.abstract: The prey choice model, widely applied in archaeological reconstructions of Pleistocene diet, predicts that people will initially focus on a narrow suite of high-ranked prey before broadening their diet to include lower-ranked species as necessitated by subsistence needs. However, evidence from arid and semiarid northern Australia challenges this assumption. Archaeological faunal records demonstrate that a broad diet was established early and persisted through the Holocene. We argue that these diverse diets do not indicate resource scarcity, but rather represent an ideal strategy for exploiting abundant, low-risk hidden, or cryptic prey, as well as high-risk, conspicuous prey within an environment characterized by unpredictable rainfall. This pattern also necessitates reconceptualizing traditional notions of prey rank and dietary breadth. Rather than adhering to static prey rankings, northern Australian peoples skillfully adapted their hunting strategies in response to fluctuating nutritional content and pursuit costs of different species. The most successful subsistence strategy in this region was therefore one of high responsiveness and flexibility, manifesting as a consistently broad diet. This case study suggests that the relationship between human dietary breadth and resource abundance is more nuanced in situations of abundant, cryptic prey.

articles_hidden.title: Gap test–inspired crack-parallel tension tests of fracture of soft-knitted polymer composites simulated by microplane triads
articles_hidden.authors: Xiaoxiao Ding, Yanzhao Niu, Yang Zhao, Hongshun Chen, Chanhyeong Bae, Anh Tay Nguyen, Horacio D. Espinosa, Zdeněk P. Bažant, Jian Cao
articles_hidden.abstract: Soft composites are increasingly used in wearable and soft robotic systems, as advances in material architecture enable greater damage tolerance under large deformation. In these mesoscale architectures, the crack-parallel stresses modify the crack initiation and growth in the opening-mode fracture. Emulating the gap test, we introduce a fracture test to quantify how the superposed crack-parallel tension affects the maximum load (i.e., the load capacity) and the load-deflection curve. A Mode I (opening mode) center-notched tensioned strip is used because its advantages in generating crack-parallel tension outweigh its hypothetical disadvantages with possible instability of crack jumps at two competing crack fronts. We develop and experimentally validate a continuum model that captures the nonlinear behavior and progressive damage of knitted composites. To this end, we introduce an ensemble of oriented microplane triads tangential to the yarn at characteristic points of the yarn loop within a repetitive unit cell of the knit. The triads ensure the yarn-polymer transfer of all normal and shear stress components at each characteristic point. The experimentally calibrated computational model provides a tool to predict the effect of crack-parallel tension on the changes of load capacity and of the effective fracture energy of knitted polymer composites, enabling rational design of these composites in engineering applications such as wearables and soft robotics.

articles_hidden.title: Conditions for runaway ruptures during reservoir operations: Magnitude–frequency distribution implications and application to Groningen
articles_hidden.authors: Qian Shi, Alexis Sáez, Linxuan Li, Kyungjae Im, Stephen Bourne, Jan van Elk, Jean-Philippe Avouac
articles_hidden.abstract: We present a theoretical analysis of an induced seismic rupture propagating from a gas reservoir into the underburden. We use linear elastic fracture mechanics to determine the conditions for self-arrested or runaway ruptures. We derive a phase diagram in which the model parameters (the reservoir thickness, the reservoir pressure depletion, background stress, and fracture energy) are combined into two dimensionless parameters. We apply the analysis to the seismicity induced by gas extraction from the Groningen gas field, where earthquakes have remained confined to the close vicinity of the reservoir. We invert the observations for the model parameters. They indicate subcritical initial stress on the underburden faults, meaning that runaway ruptures are possible in principle, but the conditions required for such events to have happened were most likely not met in reality. The model reproduces the spatial and temporal patterns of observed maximum earthquake magnitudes, and the significant deficit of M > 3.0 events compared to the expectation from the Gutenberg–Richter relationship. This tapering implies that the expected maximum magnitude is nearly insensitive to the total number of induced earthquakes and strongly controlled by the reservoir thickness and pressure depletion. Because the forecast is probabilistic and accounts for uncertainties in the model parameters, it does not exclude runaway ruptures; but such events are found to be unlikely. The model offers an operational framework to forecast earthquake magnitudes by constraining the physical model with measurable parameters.

articles_hidden.title: Structural basis of plastid Mg 2+ transport by the magnesium channel MGT10 in Arabidopsis
articles_hidden.authors: Chao Wang, Aiyan Huang, Lingjie Lin, Jinda Ou, Qiqi Zhang, Yingying Li, Chengcheng Liang, Xiumei Xu, Wei Wang, Minrui Fan, Lixin Zhang, Peiqiang Feng
articles_hidden.abstract: Magnesium ions (Mg 2+ ) are vital for photosynthesis, serving as central metal ions in chlorophyll molecules and activating RuBisCO. MGT10 is the only member of the CorA/MRS2 superfamily bound to the chloroplast envelope membrane, where it mediates Mg 2+ uptake and homeostasis in chloroplasts. Despite its importance, the mechanism of MGT10-mediated Mg 2+ transport remains unclear. Here, we report cryoelectron microscopy structures of Arabidopsis MGT10 in two conformations, along with functional characterizations. MGT10 assembles into a homopentameric structure with a central tunnel connecting the transmembrane and soluble domains. A constriction ring consisting of five conserved arginine residues arranged asymmetrically in the tunnel is crucial for Mg 2+ conduction. Our structures reveal an unexpected gating mechanism involving a conformational transition from a symmetric closed state to an asymmetric, putatively open state. In addition, we identified an intramolecular disulfide bond within each soluble domain as a unique structural feature of MGT10. Structural and functional analyses show that this disulfide bond is required for MGT10’s structural integrity and for regulating its function in photosynthesis. Taken together, our findings provide insights into Mg 2+ transport and regulatory mechanisms of MGT10 in chloroplasts.

articles_hidden.title: Breakdown of the classical rupture theory and earthquake propagation in the “forbidden” super-Rayleigh range
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Pomyalov, Fabian Barras, Eran Bouchbinder
articles_hidden.abstract: Earthquakes propagating faster than the shear wave-speed are commonly thought to undergo a supershear transition upon which they discontinuously jump from the sub-Rayleigh regime to the supershear one. The super-Rayleigh regime, i.e., the range of propagation speeds between the Rayleigh and shear wave-speeds, is regarded as “forbidden” by the two-dimensional classical rupture theory. Here, we revisit the assumptions underlying the classical theory and develop a rupture theory that takes into account the dependence of the fault strength (frictional resistance) on the slip rate. The theory quantitatively agrees with numerical simulations nearly up to the Rayleigh wave-speed. Yet, very close to the latter, numerical rupture solutions change their character due to frictional rate nonlinearity, involving rate-strengthening friction, and rupture continuously propagates through the “forbidden” super-Rayleigh range into the supershear regime, without a sharp supershear transition. These results demonstrate that frictional rate dependence, generically observed in experiments, can have profound implications for fast earthquake propagation.
